newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea retreats on labour law, strikes to continue.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea retreats on labour law, strikes to continue.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam, conceding public anxiety and damage to the economy, agreed on Tuesday to send a controversial labour law back to parliament in a stunning concession to the opposition.
At a meeting with his chief political rivals, Kim expressed sorrow for output losses of billions of dollars through strikes sparked by forced passage of the controversial bill.
Production losses from stoppages have been estimated at more than $3 billion.
Labour strife had defeated the law's aim of revitalising a sluggish economy, he said.
Kim also agreed to reopen debate on another controversial law reviving a once notorious domestic spy agency.

And, in a further about-face, he told heads of three main political parties he would instruct officials to suspend arrest warrants served on strike leaders, seven of whom are sheltering in Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral.

According to an account of the meeting by opposition leader Kim Dae-jung of the National Congress for New Politics, Kim also indicated the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions should be recognised.
Multiple trade union representation is a major demand of international labour organisations.
Kim Dae-jung welcomed Kim's retreat from his hardline stance. But the confederation said strikes would continue if the government did not declare the law null and void.
Confederation president Kwon Young-kil, holed up in the cathedral, told a news conference: "Talks today have not solved any of the basic problems."
He threatened to bring out 200,000 workers in all sectors except public services on Wednesday.
But in a further sign of compromise, police eased their security cordon around the cathedral.
Kim's dramatic climbdown followed a decision by the confederation to call off indefinite stoppages and limit industrial action to one day each week.

"Anything can be discussed in parliament again, whether it is the labour law or the law on the Agency for National Security Planning," a spokesman quoted Kim as saying during a lunch meeting in the Presidential Blue House.
Both laws were rammed through parliament in a six-minute dawn session on December 26 while opposition deputies slept.
President Kim previously insisted the laws could not be altered and rejected demands by the opposition for dialogue.

Nevertheless, it was clear hard political bargaining lay ahead. Unions and opposition parties were adamant the labour law be scrapped, but Kim insisted that dumping the legislation would go against the constitution and it could only be revised.
The law makes it easier for firms to sack workers and replace strikers. It keeps a ban on freedom of union association by delaying recognition of the confederation until 2000.

Political analysts said the law was a major gaffe by president Kim and the climbdown would erode his authority in his last year in office and damage the ruling party ahead of presidential elections in December.
"This probably is the biggest blunder of Kim's presidency," said political science professor Shin Jung-hyun. "The blunder will increase pressure to turn him into a lame duck."
Kim Dae-jung appeared taken aback by the abrupt retreat.

"Today's meeting was not a total solution but there was some advance and President Kim Young-sam showed an attitude of wanting to solve the problems together with opposition parties," he told a news conference.

He said he had complained that the security law would intimidate journalists, workers and opposition politicians, to which the president replied: "Then revise the national security law too". Kim Dae-jung added: "I was very surprised at this."
The opposition leader quoted the president as saying it was wrong to continue shunning the confederation, which claims half a million members.
"It is wrong to say it doesn't exist when it does exist in reality," Kim was quoted as saying.

After he took office in 1993, Kim Young-sam clipped the wings of the spy agency that once hounded dissidents. The new law restores its powers of investigation, ostensibly to combat subversion from communist North Korea.

The spokesman quoted the president as saying the laws "had made the situation in our economy more difficult, causing public anxiety". The president added: "The purpose of politics is to make people comfortable."
